design_detail: Two-step individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis of 18 record-linkage cohorts from the Mortality After Release from Incarceration Consortium (MARIC): cohorts of everyone released from incarceration during each study period (none built on a health condition or offence type), linked to national or state death registers. 1,471,526 people released 1980–2018 in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 10,534,441 person-years; 75,427 deaths. Each cohort team applied a common statistical analysis plan and returned aggregate counts, person-time, crude mortality rates (CMRs) and age- and sex-adjusted Cox hazard ratios; the central team pooled them by random-effects meta-analysis (Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation for confidence intervals), pooled incidence rate ratios (IRRs) between periods after release, ran univariable meta-regression on sex, age and region, and ran sensitivity analyses (excluding time reincarcerated; restricting to the ten cohorts that could separate deaths in custody from release-day deaths; leave-one-out). Rates only: there is no general-population comparison.
can_establish: Crude death rates, causes as coded in death registers, and timing of death after release from incarceration in these 18 mostly high-income cohorts; how rates differ by time since release, sex, age and region; and that deaths in custody recorded as release-day deaths inflate day-1 estimates.
cannot_establish: How far these rates exceed those of the general population (no standardized mortality ratios or comparison group), why deaths cluster soon after release (tolerance, drug use, treatment and the drug supply were not measured), which drugs were involved (the poisoning category combines alcohol and other drugs, of unintentional and undetermined intent, with no toxicology), or how accurate and comparable cause-of-death coding was across eight countries and four decades.

sample.recruitment: Registry. Correctional release records linked with national or state death registers. The MARIC consortium (30 cohorts; 1,502,007 adults released 1980–2018 in 12 mostly high-income countries) was assembled from a literature search in March 2016 and colleagues' suggestions; 29 of its 30 cohorts had linked incarceration data with death registers. The 18 cohorts analysed here, 98% of the consortium, are those of unselected releases: USA 5 (Washington, New York, Pennsylvania, North Carolina ×2), Australia 5 (Western Australia ×3, New South Wales, Queensland), Canada 3 (Ontario ×2, British Columbia), New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and Brazil (Mato Grosso do Sul) 1 each (p. 1780; Table 1, p. 1782).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cohorts: unselected samples of everyone released during the study period (cohorts built on a specific health condition or previous criminal-justice involvement excluded); reasons for each cohort's inclusion or exclusion are in appendix pp 4–7 (not read). Individuals excluded if not released during the study period or if the recorded release date was after the recorded date of death. Follow-up starts at release from the first incarceration in the study period (index incarceration); for 'any incarceration' analyses all later post-release time at risk is added, minus time reincarcerated (p. 1781, Data analysis, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: 88.3% men (sex recorded by corrections as male or female); median age at release 26–36 years by cohort (age for the Brazilian cohort from a subset of 2393 only); median follow-up 3.1–18.1 years by cohort, range 0–24 years; one cohort (Rosen, North Carolina) men only (Table 1, p. 1782). Race and ethnicity were not analysed (p. 1786).
sample.attrition: Loss to follow-up (emigration, failed linkage, deaths outside the registers' coverage) is not discussed. Two cohorts (Binswanger; Cunningham and King) could not provide some cause-specific data or deaths by day; 640 deaths had a missing cause (Table 2 footnotes, p. 1784; Figure 2 legend, p. 1785).
sample.selection_effects: Almost entirely high-income countries (one Brazilian cohort); cohorts exist only where release records could be linked to death registers. The index release was often not a person's first (earlier records unavailable), and risk is said to rise with each release. The authors suggest US cohorts may be less selected because incarceration thresholds are lower there ('inverse selection'). Cohort crude rates range from 236 per 100,000 person-years (Lim, New York, 244,274 people) to 1183 (Fazel and Chang, Sweden). Three Western Australian cohorts (Giles 2005–2014, Preen A 1994–2003, Preen B 1985–2008) overlap in place and period; whether any person or death appears in more than one cohort is not addressed in the main text (Table 1; Figure 1).

exposure.measurement: Release from incarceration, with release and reincarceration dates, from correctional records. Deaths and underlying causes from linked national or state death registers, grouped from ICD-9 or ICD-10 underlying-cause codes into a two-level, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive system (code list in appendix p 8, not read) (pp. 1780–1781).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. No drug use, treatment in custody (including opioid agonist treatment), sentence length or pre-release health data were analysed; only age, sex, region and time since release.
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured. The 'alcohol and other drug poisoning' category (unintentional and undetermined intent) does not separate drugs, alcohol or combinations, and no toxicology is reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not measured. Time since release is the only proxy for a break in use; tolerance and drug use before or after release were not recorded.

comparison.controls: Internal only: periods after release (days 2–14 daily, weeks 3–12 weekly, weeks 13–52, week 53 onward, total follow-up), sex, age groups and regions; index release against any release. No general-population comparison and no standardized mortality ratios.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Hazard ratios adjusted for age and sex only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Substance use disorders, mental illness, treatment, prior incarcerations, sentence length, race and ethnicity were unavailable or not analysed (Limitations, p. 1786).

outcomes.instruments: All-cause and cause-specific mortality from the death-register underlying cause (ICD-9 or ICD-10). Table 2 categories: maternal, nutritional and infectious (HIV; respiratory infections; tuberculosis; maternal; other); non-communicable (cardiovascular; cancer; liver; chronic respiratory; diabetes; other); injuries (alcohol and other drug poisoning of unintentional and undetermined intent; suicide; interpersonal violence; transport; other); other and ill-defined (intermediate and immediate causes; ill-defined or unknown); missing cause.
outcomes.validity_norms: The validity and comparability of cause-of-death certification and coding across countries and decades are not assessed. Inspection of the data showed that in some cohorts deaths in custody had been coded as occurring on the day of release; ten cohorts could separate the two definitively, eight could not (pp. 1781, 1786).
outcomes.operationalization: A drug death here is a death whose underlying cause is coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning of unintentional or undetermined intent; where intentional self-poisoning was classed is not stated in the main text (code list in appendix p 8). The Discussion calls these 'overdose deaths' (p. 1784). Who certified causes, whether autopsy or toxicology was done, and in what share of deaths, are not reported. Primary analyses start observation on day 2 (the first full 24 hours after release) because of the release-day coding problem.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The 24 rows of Table 2 (all-cause, categories and subcategories) are each estimated overall and, mostly in the appendix, by period after release, sex, age group and region; statements of significance (for example men's higher cardiovascular and transport death rates) are not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (registry outcomes). Cohort teams applied the common analysis plan; one named author accessed and verified the data and performed all meta-analyses (Contributors, p. 1787).

analysis.effect_sizes: Per 100,000 person-years, random-effects pooled CMRs with 95% CIs. All-cause after the index release 725 (625–831), I² 100% in the text and Figure 1, 98.8% in Table 2; men 731 (630–839), women 660 (560–767), meta-regression p=0.330; cohort CMRs 236 to 1183. Days 2–7: all-cause 1612 (1048–2287), I² 91.1%; more than 1 year: 737 (636–844). IRR of the first week against week 2 1.5 (1.2–1.8), I² 26.0%; against weeks 3–4 2.0 (1.5–2.6), I² 53.0%; against weeks 9–12 2.2 (1.6–3.0), I² 70.5%. Days 2–7 by cause: alcohol and other drug (AOD) poisoning 657 (332–1076), I² 89.0%; suicide 135 (36–277); cardiovascular disease 71 (16–153). Whole follow-up: AOD poisoning 146 (103–197), I² 99.7%, 16,126 deaths; cardiovascular 102 (85–119); cancer 74 (61–88); suicide 67 (49–87); interpersonal violence 50 (32–72); transport 43 (33–56); all injuries 371 (310–438); non-communicable diseases 261 (220–306). Days 2–7 by region: Europe 2762 (1832–3872), USA 934 (389–1703). AOD poisoning by region: Europe 292 (258–329), Brazil 16 (12–22). Sensitivity: excluding reincarceration time (16 cohorts) 720 (605–845); ten cohorts able to separate custody deaths, overall 693 (557–845) and release-day CMR 826 (0–3455) against 4036 (887–8940); days 2–7 after any release 2460 (1516–3618); leave-one-out 701 (604–805) without the Swedish cohort and 762 (690–838) without the New York cohort. Absolute: 14,671 of 16,126 (91.0%) AOD poisoning deaths occurred more than 4 weeks after release. No prediction intervals; no standardized mortality ratios.
analysis.covariates: Crude rates are unadjusted. Cox hazard ratios from univariable models and multivariable models with age and sex only, pooled by random effects; reported in the appendix (p 31) and summarized as no association between sex and all-cause mortality.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A study protocol was published (Borschmann et al., 2020, Int J Popul Data Sci 5:1145; not read) and the statistical analysis plan is available on request (p. 1787). The article itself states that aggregation of weeks after the first two was decided post hoc and that observation was started on day 2 after inspection of release-day data (p. 1781); whether other analyses depart from the protocol cannot be judged without it.
analysis.selective_reporting: Most stratified results (age, cause by region, cause by period) are only in the appendix, which was not read. The Summary reports the first-week peak but not that 91.0% of the poisoning deaths occurred more than 4 weeks after release, nor the release-day coding artefact; both are in the main text.
analysis.power: Large overall (75,427 deaths), but estimates for single days and for days 2–7 have wide intervals (all-cause 1048–2287; AOD poisoning 332–1076), and the daily estimates in Figure 2A overlap widely with each other and with later periods.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 18 cohorts, crude death rates were highest on days 2–7 after release (all-cause 1612 per 100,000 person-years; alcohol and other drug poisoning 657), fell over the following week, and then stayed roughly level at about 700–860 per 100,000 from week 3 onward (Figure 2A, read approximately). Poisoning was the leading cause over the whole follow-up (146 per 100,000; 21.4% of deaths), but 91.0% of poisoning deaths occurred more than 4 weeks after release. Rates differed greatly between cohorts (236 to 1183) and regions (I² near 100%). Release-day estimates were inflated by deaths in custody recorded as release-day deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary says the markedly elevated death rate in the first week underscores an urgent need for coordinated transitional care to prevent post-release deaths from suicide and overdose (p. 1779). The first-week peak is supported, but: most poisoning deaths happened later, as the authors themselves say when noting that acute prevention would prevent only a small minority (p. 1784); the comparison with the general population that the Background invokes is not made in this study; the poisoning category identifies neither opioids nor any other drug; and nothing about tolerance, drug use or treatment was measured, so neither the cause of the early peak nor the effect of any intervention is shown. The Results say the all-cause rate 'decreased consistently' to 737 more than a year after release (p. 1783), but Figure 2A shows a plateau after about the first week, with the rate beyond a year slightly above the overall pooled rate of 725. The calls for medications for opioid use disorder and naloxone at release (p. 1786) rest on other evidence.

timeline.event: Pratt et al., population-based cohort of suicide in recently released prisoners (ref. 11), cited among studies showing markedly elevated death rates after release compared with the general population (not read).

Binswanger et al., NEJM, release from prison and the risk of death (ref. 10); a Washington State cohort led by Binswanger is one of the 18 pooled here (Table 1), so the two are not independent (not read).

Kinner et al., estimate of deaths among recently released prisoners in Australia (ref. 18), cited for lower death rates during incarceration, the reason for the reincarceration sensitivity analysis (not read).
Kinner, Forsyth & Williams, systematic review of record-linkage studies of mortality in ex-prisoners: why (good) methods matter (ref. 12; on the project's General list; not read).
MARIC cohorts identified through a literature search (March 2016) and colleagues' suggestions.
Forsyth et al., Australian prospective cohort (ref. 28), cited for a rising risk of death with each subsequent release (not read).
MARIC protocol published (Borschmann et al., Int J Popul Data Sci 5:1145; ref. 15; not read).
This IPD meta-analysis, published with a linked Comment in the same issue (Lancet 2024;403:1727–1729; not among the files read).

replication.where_it_stands: The largest pooled description of death after release from incarceration. It confirms a first-week peak in these cohorts and shows that earlier day-1 peaks are partly a coding artefact. It pools cohorts that were published separately (for example Binswanger's Washington cohort), and earlier meta-analyses of drug-related deaths soon after release (Merrall et al., 2010, on the project's _Tolerance list; not read) may share cohorts with it, so it should not be counted as independent replication of them. It reports crude rates only: the excess over the general population and the role of lost tolerance must come from other studies.

funding.funder: MARIC: Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC; GNT1120004). Bukten and Clausen cohort: The South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority (grant number 2019091) and The Norwegian Research Council (grant number 301535). The paper states that the funder had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (pp. 1779, 1781, 1787).
funding.declared_conflicts: As declared (p. 1787): RB, salary and research support from an NHMRC Emerging Leadership-2 Investigator Grant (EL2; GNT2008073); MJS, Australian Research Council Future Fellowship (project number FT180100075), funded by the Australian Government; SLa, research scholar award from Fonds de recherche du Québec–Santé; JRA, US National Institutes of Health (R01 AI130058); RC, PK and KT, a University of Otago research grant; all other authors, no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: Byline authors from the University of Melbourne, the University of Oxford, the Murdoch Children's Research Institute, Curtin University and Griffith University (p. 1779); the collaborators include the cohort investigators, who analysed their own cohorts under the common plan, as the IPD design requires. Data stewards (Washington Department of Corrections, Western Australian Department of Justice, British Columbia, Stats NZ) disclaim endorsement (Acknowledgments, p. 1787). Individual participant data will not be shared. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Linked release cohorts that record, for each release, recent drug use and treatment in custody (including opioid agonist treatment), with toxicology for every post-release death (drugs and concentrations), consistent cause-of-death coding across jurisdictions, reliable separation of deaths in custody from release-day deaths, and standardized mortality ratios against the general population by time since release.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (everyone released from incarceration in unselected cohorts), strata (time since release, sex, age, region) and outcomes (all-cause and cause-specific death) are stated; comparisons are internal, which suits the descriptive aim; there is no general-population comparator.

The article says a protocol was published previously (Borschmann et al., 2020) and the analysis plan is available on request; neither was read. Two departures are declared (aggregation of weeks after week 2 decided post hoc; observation from day 2 after inspecting the data). Whether the protocol set out the search, criteria and a risk-of-bias plan, and whether it preceded cohort identification in 2016, cannot be judged from the article.
Restriction to cohorts of everyone released (not built on a health condition or offence) is explained as a way to increase generalisability (p. 1780).

Cohorts were identified through a 'comprehensive search of the literature' in March 2016 and colleagues' suggestions, with details in the protocol (not read); the article gives no databases, terms or restrictions and reports no update after 2016. The Research-in-context search (MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, English, to 1 February 2023) is a background search, not the cohort search. A search about seven years older than publication rules out 'yes'; partial yes or no depends on the protocol.

How cohorts were screened, and by how many reviewers, is not described in the article; the 18 of 30 consortium cohorts were chosen by a stated rule (unselected releases), with reasons in appendix pp 4–7 (not read).

IPD process: each cohort team applied the common analysis plan to its own data and returned aggregate outputs, and a central author accessed and verified the data (Contributors, p. 1787). Not duplicate extraction in the usual sense, but data produced by one team were checked by another; judged met, a close call.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for cohort inclusion and exclusion are in appendix pp 4–7 (p. 1781), which was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives each cohort's country or state, dates, size, sex split, median age, follow-up, person-years and deaths; how each cohort was linked to death records, linkage quality and ICD version are not in the article.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or data-quality appraisal of the cohorts is described in the Methods or listed among the appendix contents; linkage completeness, death-register coverage, cause-of-death certification and coding were not assessed. The release-day artefact was found by inspecting the data, not by a planned appraisal.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding of the individual cohorts is not reported, except for the Norwegian cohort (Acknowledgments).

Random-effects pooling of cohort CMRs (Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation for intervals), of IRRs and of log hazard ratios, with meta-regression and leave-one-out analyses. Weaknesses not scored by this item: with I² of 98.8–100% the random-effects weights are almost equal (5.50–5.58% per cohort, Figure 1), so the pooled CMR is close to an unweighted average of very different cohorts and describes no particular population; no prediction intervals; a transformation for proportions is applied to deaths per person-time.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses tested the two data problems the authors identified (deaths during reincarceration: 720 vs 725; deaths in custody coded as release-day deaths, restricting to ten cohorts: 693 vs 725 overall, 826 vs 4036 on the day of release) and the influence of each cohort (leave-one-out, 701 to 762). No analysis examined cause-of-death misclassification.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion treats the release-day artefact carefully, but interprets cause-specific and regional rates (for example the highest AOD poisoning rate in Europe and the lowest in Brazil) through selection and context alone, without considering differences in death certification, toxicology practice and coding of drug deaths and undetermined intent across eight countries and four decades.

I² is reported for each estimate; meta-regression by sex, age and region and leave-one-out analyses were done, and regional differences are discussed (inverse selection in the USA; violence in Brazil; the effect of missing low- and middle-income cohorts).

Not investigated or discussed. In an IPD consortium analysed under one plan, selective publication of results matters less, but which jurisdictions have linkable records and joined the consortium is examined only as the scarcity of low- and middle-income cohorts.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the funder's role and authors' interests are declared (pp. 1781, 1787).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 2, 4, 5 and 7 can be judged only from the published protocol (Borschmann et al., 2020) and the appendix (pp 4–7), neither of which was read; the overall rating does not depend on them. Three critical items are not met in the article itself: no appraisal of the cohorts' data quality or risk of bias (9), no account of cause-of-death misclassification or coding differences when interpreting cause-specific and regional rates (13), and no investigation of publication or availability bias (15). Under AMSTAR 2, more than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence; a reader who set item 15 aside as unsuited to an IPD consortium would still find two. The rating concerns how far the pooled rates are unbiased summaries; it does not question the study's size or internal care (a common analysis plan, sensitivity analyses that exposed the release-day artefact, leave-one-out checks). Cite it for crude rates, causes as coded and timing of death after release in these cohorts, the first-week peak, the 91% share of poisoning deaths after 4 weeks, and the release-day coding artefact; not for excess mortality relative to the general population, for which drugs were involved, or for lost tolerance as the mechanism.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 18 cohorts (98% of the 30-cohort MARIC consortium) of everyone released from incarceration in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA, 1980–2018: 1,471,526 people (1,299,322 men, 88.3%; 172,204 women, 11.7%), 10,534,441 person-years and 75,427 deaths (5.1%).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and data sources, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 1780); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1781); Table 1 (p. 1782)

key_findings.finding: How deaths were counted: by linkage of correctional records with national or state death registers; causes are the underlying cause of death in ICD-9 or ICD-10, grouped into a two-level, mutually exclusive system (codes in appendix p 8); drug deaths are the category 'alcohol and other drug poisoning (unintentional and undetermined intent)'. Who certified causes and whether autopsy or toxicology was done are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and data sources, 2nd paragraph (p. 1780); Methods › Data analysis, 3rd paragraph (p. 1781); Table 2 (p. 1784)

key_findings.finding: All-cause pooled crude mortality after release from the index incarceration: 725 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 625–831), I² 100% (text, Figure 1) or 98.8% (Table 2); men 731 (630–839), women 660 (560–767), no difference on meta-regression (p=0.330); rates similar up to age 34 and rising with age after that. Cohort rates ranged from 236 (Lim, New York) to 1183 (Fazel and Chang, Sweden).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1781, continuing on p. 1782); Figure 1 (p. 1783); Table 2 (p. 1784)

key_findings.finding: Causes over the whole follow-up: alcohol and other drug (AOD) poisoning was the leading cause, CMR 146 (103–197), I² 99.7%, 16,126 deaths (21.4% of all deaths); then cardiovascular disease 102 (85–119) and cancer 74 (61–88). Injuries accounted for 37,425 deaths (printed as 49.7%), CMR 371 (310–438), including suicide (6199 deaths, 8.2%; CMR 67, 49–87) and interpersonal violence (6361, 8.4%; CMR 50, 32–72); non-communicable diseases 29,731 (39.4%); infectious diseases 3597 (4.8%).

Timing: the all-cause CMR was highest on days 2–7 after release, 1612 (1048–2287), I² 91.1%, against 737 (636–844) more than 1 year after release; pooled incidence rate ratios for the first week were 1.5 (1.2–1.8) against week 2, 2.0 (1.5–2.6) against weeks 3–4 and 2.2 (1.6–3.0) against weeks 9–12.

Days 2–7 by cause: AOD poisoning CMR 657 (332–1076), I² 89.0%; suicide 135 (36–277); cardiovascular disease 71 (16–153). AOD poisoning had the highest rate of any cause in the first 2 weeks and the highest point estimate in every period examined, and was the only cause whose rate peaked in the first week; cancer deaths peaked after more than 1 year (77, 63–93).

Shape of the curve (Figure 2A, all-cause, values read approximately from the plotted points): about 1900 per 100,000 person-years on day 2 and about 1600 on day 3, about 1000–1200 on days 4–8, about 500–800 on days 9–14, and about 700–860 in each period from weeks 3–4 to week 53 onward; the daily intervals are wide and overlap the later periods.
key_findings.note: No values are printed in the figure; read on a 300-dpi rendering, approximate to about ±50. Figure 2 excludes two cohorts (Cunningham and King; Binswanger) without deaths-by-day data.

key_findings.finding: 14,671 (91.0%) of the 16,126 AOD poisoning deaths, which the Discussion calls 'overdose deaths', occurred more than 4 weeks after release; the authors conclude that acute post-release prevention would prevent only a small minority of these deaths and that sustained treatment and harm reduction are needed.
key_findings.note: The share mainly reflects that most person-time lies beyond 4 weeks (median follow-up 3.1–18.1 years by cohort), while the rate per person-year is highest in the first week; both hold at once.

key_findings.finding: Release-day coding artefact: inspection of the data suggested that in some cohorts deaths in custody had been coded as deaths on the day of release; ten cohorts could separate the two definitively, eight could not. Restricted to the ten, the release-day CMR fell from 4036 (887–8940) to 826 (0–3455) and the overall CMR was 693 (557–845) against 725. Primary analyses therefore started observation on day 2.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data analysis, 6th–7th paragraphs (p. 1781); Results, 9th paragraph (p. 1783); Discussion, 8th paragraph (p. 1786)

key_findings.finding: Reincarceration: in the 16 cohorts with reincarceration data (1,309,958 people, 8,324,428 person-years, 56,731 deaths), excluding time and deaths while reincarcerated gave an all-cause CMR of 720 (605–845), almost identical to 725. The days 2–7 rate after any release, 2460 (1516–3618), was numerically higher than after the index release, 1612, but not significantly on meta-regression.

Regions: the days 2–7 all-cause CMR was highest in Europe, 2762 (1832–3872), and lowest in the USA, 934 (389–1703), with no regional difference after more than 1 year. Over the whole follow-up, AOD poisoning was highest in Europe, 292 (258–329), and lowest in the Brazilian cohort, 16 (12–22), where interpersonal violence was highest, 299 (281–319); suicide was highest in Australia and New Zealand, 103 (81–128). The authors suggest 'inverse selection' (lower incarceration thresholds in the USA) for the low US rates.
Leave-one-out: the largest changes from the primary estimate of 725 came from removing the Swedish cohort, 701 (604–805), and the New York cohort, 762 (690–838).

Limitations stated by the authors: the index release was probably not the first for many people; almost all cohorts were from high-income countries; only age and sex were examined (no race or ethnicity; sex recorded as binary); nothing was known about what happened between release and death; sentence length was not examined; eight cohorts could not separate deaths in custody from release-day deaths.

The authors call for health assessment at prison reception, care equivalent to the community including medications for opioid use disorder, pre-release planning that includes naloxone for people who have had opioid use disorder, and routine monitoring of post-release mortality; none of these was measured or evaluated in the study.

reporting_issues.issue: Heterogeneity for the same all-cause estimate (725, 625–831) is given as I² 100% in the Results text and Figure 1 and as 98.8% in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both mean near-total between-cohort heterogeneity.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the Brazilian (Liu) cohort's women as 7215 (1.6%) of 62,425, against 55,210 men (88.4%); editors' calculation: 7215 of 62,425 is 11.6%, consistent with the printed share of men.

Table 1 column totals for sex and person-time do not equal the sums of the rows: the printed totals are 172,204 women, 1,299,322 men and 10,534,441 person-years, while sample sizes and deaths add up exactly. Editors' calculation from the printed rows (checked on a 300-dpi rendering): 172,564 women and 1,298,962 men, a difference of 360 each way, and 10,534,666 person-years.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small, but the sex split and person-time used in the Summary and Results cannot be reproduced from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say the all-cause rate 'decreased consistently' after the first week to 737 (636–844) more than 1 year after release, but Figure 2A shows lower daily rates on days 9–14 (about 500–800) than in weeks 3–4 (about 860) and a level of about 700–860 from week 3 onward; 737 is above the overall pooled rate of 725.
reporting_issues.consequence: The excess is concentrated in roughly the first week rather than declining steadily; the wording overstates a gradient.

reporting_issues.issue: Injury deaths are printed as 37,425 (49.7%) of 75,427 deaths; editors' calculation: the share is 49.6%.

Table 2 does not add up exactly, which a footnote attributes to cohorts that could not provide some causes; the denominator for each cause is not given. Editors' calculation: the cause categories sum to 75,417 rather than 75,427, and the infectious subcategories to 3612 against a category total of 3679 (the text's 3597 equals the subcategories without the 15 maternal deaths).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cause-specific rates come from slightly different sets of cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: Follow-up per person is described as ranging from 1 month to 24 years (p. 1780, for the consortium) but as 0–24 years in the Summary and from 0.0 years in every cohort of Table 1.

The Discussion calls the AOD poisoning category 'overdose deaths' and links it to opioid use disorder treatment and naloxone, but the category includes alcohol poisoning and deaths of undetermined intent and identifies no drug.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures cannot be cited as opioid overdose deaths; claims about opioids need other sources.

reporting_issues.issue: Three Western Australian cohorts (Giles 2005–2014; Preen A 1994–2003; Preen B 1985–2008) overlap in place and period; the main text does not say whether any person or death appears in more than one cohort (cohort descriptions are in appendix pp 4–7, not read).
reporting_issues.consequence: If they overlap, some deaths would count twice in pooled estimates; this cannot be settled without the appendix.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Lancet 2024;403:1779–1788, all pages (Summary, Research in context, Methods, Results, Tables 1–2, Figures 1–2, Discussion, collaborators, contributors, declarations, data sharing, acknowledgments and references); tables and figures checked on rendered pages, Table 1 and Figure 2A also at 300 dpi. The online appendix, the published protocol (Borschmann et al., 2020) and the linked Comment (Lancet 2024;403:1727–1729) were not among the files and were not read.
